nodes.blurb: Rice, broth and broccoli in one pot, with the cheese stirred in at the end off the heat. Nothing to drain, nothing to time precisely, and the broccoli goes soft enough that nobody argues with it.

nodes.label: Three-Ingredient Banana Oat Pancakes
nodes.blurb: Oats, banana and egg blended into a batter. No flour, no sugar, and they taste like banana bread — which is what happens when the only sweetness is fruit that was going brown anyway.

nodes.label: Yogurt Bowls with Toasted Oat Crunch
nodes.blurb: Five minutes of toasting turns rolled oats and almonds into something with real crunch, and it keeps for two weeks in a jar. After that this is a breakfast a six-year-old can make alone.

nodes.label: Egg in a Hole with Wilted Greens
nodes.blurb: A piece of toast with an egg cooked into the middle of it, and a handful of spinach wilted in the same pan while the egg sets. Six minutes, one pan, and the cut-out circle is the best bit.

nodes.label: Smashed Cucumbers with Sesame and Rice Vinegar
nodes.blurb: Cucumbers hit with the flat of a knife until they crack open, then dressed. Smashing instead of slicing gives the dressing rough edges to hold onto, which is why this tastes so much stronger than a sliced cucumber salad.

nodes.label: Black Bean and Corn Salad
nodes.blurb: Opened, drained, tipped in, squeezed over. A child of eight can make this entirely alone, and it is still the bowl that empties first at a cookout.

nodes.label: Apple Boats with Peanut Butter and Crunch
nodes.blurb: Apple wedges hollowed slightly, filled with peanut butter, and loaded with whatever is crunchy. The after-school snack that actually holds somebody until dinner.

nodes.label: Two-Minute Berry Banana Soft Serve
nodes.blurb: Frozen banana blended until it stops being a fruit and starts being ice cream. There is no dairy in it and nothing added, and it genuinely works — the trick is patience with the blender.

edges.note: One clove is about an eighth of a teaspoon of powder. Powder has no bite and cannot be browned, so it suits rubs and dry mixes rather than a pan.
Flakes bring heat but none of the green, vegetal flavor of a fresh chile.
Peppery rather than neutral, and it wilts — dress it at the table.
Ground ginger is warmer and less bright. It works in a braise or a bake, not in a dressing.
Dried basil is for cooking into a sauce, not for finishing — add it early and it has time to open up.
Thyme is milder and less resinous than rosemary — a fair swap in a braise, less so where rosemary is the point.
Dried thyme is more concentrated than fresh, so this is about a third of the volume. Add it early rather than at the end.
Crumble it and press out the water first. It scrambles, but it will not set or bind.
Savory and cheesy, but it will not melt or brown. Use it as a finish, not inside a bake.
Fine in a batter or a pan. Not in anything that needs butter to be solid — pastry, creaming, or browning.
Dry lentils need about 25 minutes of simmering and enough extra liquid to cover them.
Canned beans are already cooked, so add them near the end rather than at the start.
Add about two cups of extra liquid and 25 minutes. Brown the aromatics harder to make up the savor.
Cocoa is chocolate with the fat taken out — add about a tablespoon of butter or oil per ounce of chocolate replaced.
A liquid sweetener where a dry one was: take about three tablespoons of other liquid out per cup, and expect a softer bake.
Paste brings the same concentrated tomato but none of the chew.
You lose the sweetness and the vinegar. A pinch of sugar and a splash of vinegar gets most of it back.
Powder needs frying in oil for a minute to wake up; paste does not.
Fresh basil goes in off the heat. Cooked, it turns gray and loses most of what you wanted from it.
Add the sprigs whole and fish them out at the end.
Fresh garlic is far milder by weight than powder — about two cloves per teaspoon. Cook it in fat for a minute or it stays raw and harsh.
Fresh onion brings water with it — give it a few minutes in the pan before the rest of the recipe carries on.
Fresh ginger is mostly water, so it takes several times the weight of the ground. Grate it rather than chopping.
Turmeric gives the color and none of the perfume. It is a stand-in for the look, not the taste.
Sumac is dried lemon, essentially. Zest plus a squeeze of juice covers it.
Paprika plus cayenne gets the color and heat; you lose the fenugreek and the warm spices that make berbere itself.
Powdered sugar has cornstarch in it and dissolves cold. Granulated will stay gritty in an icing.
Dried cranberries are sweetened, so cut the sugar in the recipe by about half.
A real change of flavor, not just of form. Sage is what makes brown butter taste like brown butter.
Smoked paprika carries the smoke but almost no heat.
The crunch is the point of chili crisp and flakes have none of it. Fry them in a spoonful of oil with a sliced garlic clove.
Only for cooked applications. Falafel needs raw soaked chickpeas and canned ones will fall apart.
Chili powder is a blend with cumin and oregano already in it, so go easy on those elsewhere in the recipe.
Same volume, but it will not thicken and it can split if you boil it. Take the pan off the heat before it goes in.
Soak them in boiling water for 15 minutes and blend with an equal volume of water until completely smooth.
Stir a tablespoon of vinegar or lemon juice into a cup of milk and let it sit five minutes. It curdles, which is the point.
Nonfat Greek yogurt swaps one for one cold. Off the heat only — it splits if you boil it.
Cream cheese is tangier and stiffer. Loosen it with a spoonful of cream and it stands in for mascarpone in a cold dessert.
Soy sauce plus a few drops of vinegar. Standard Worcestershire contains anchovy, so this is also the vegetarian swap.
You lose the heat and the acidity — add a squeeze of lemon.
Light has about a third the fat. Fine in a curry; it will not whip and it will not set a dessert.
Balsamic is sweeter and less smoky, but it is the closest thing in an American pantry.
Dry sherry is closer, dry white wine is fine. Skip the salted 'cooking wine' at the grocery store.
Halve the amount and add a splash of rice vinegar — mirin is sweet but also acidic and much less concentrated than honey.
Soy plus a squeeze of lime gets most of the way there for a vegetarian table. A teaspoon of white miso adds the funk back.
Lime brings the sourness but none of the raisiny depth. Add a teaspoon of brown sugar with it.
Balsamic reduced by half is the closest substitute — sweet, thick and sour in the same proportions.
Butter burns where ghee does not — keep the heat lower if you swap.
Italian pepper flakes are hotter and less fruity. Use half and you land in the right place.
Walnuts in pesto are the traditional Ligurian thrift move, not a compromise.
